Keeping a harbour ledger by hand

Why one small port still writes its tide readings in ink, and what the habit teaches the people who keep it.

The harbour office at Wexmoor keeps its tide readings in a bound ledger, and has done so since before the lighthouse was built. Every reading is written in ink by whoever is on watch, with the time, the height of the water at the gauge and a word about the weather.

Visitors often ask why the office does not simply let the radar gauge post its numbers to a screen. The harbour master's answer is that the ledger is read as well as written: a keeper who writes the readings down notices when the tide runs late, and asks why.

The habit has a cost. Copying a year's readings into a fresh volume takes most of a week each spring, and the office has twice lost a page to a leaking window. But the ledgers have also settled two disputes over mooring fees and one over a dredging contract.

Other ports along the coast gave up their ledgers decades ago, and several of their harbour masters say they miss them.
